messages.author: 8c8f0ca54c4a2459
messages.subject: Numbering consecutive blocks
parts:
I have a data set in which I want to count consecutive sets of special values, like so:

```
df = data.frame(Block = c(1000, 2000, 380, rpois(3, 50), 2000, 1000, rpois(5, 30), 1000))
df
```
```
   Block
1   1000
2   2000
3    380
4     63
5     58
6     35
7   2000
8   1000
9     34
10    27
11    33
12    32
13    26
14  1000
```

100, 2000, and 380 are special values, I want to count and label contiguous "Sets" of these  values, and get this:

```
   Block Set
1   1000   1
2   2000   1
3    380   1
4     60   0
5     50   0
6     47   0
7   2000   2
8   1000   2
9     20   0
10    27   0
11    27   0
12    36   0
13    40   0
14  1000   3
```

+1 for a `dplyr`-based solution.

messages.author: 8d1674b7b16af1b1
messages.subject: Re: [D-RUG]: Numbering consecutive blocks
parts:
special = c(1000, 2000, 380)

# Find special values, convert to run-length encoding
rl = rle(df[,1] %in% special)

# Change TRUEs to sequential integers
rl$values[rl$values] = 1:sum(rl$values)

# Convert back to the original encoding and add as a column to df
cbind(df, set = inverse.rle(rl))

messages.author: b35e99045f6c74c2
messages.subject: Re: [D-RUG]: Numbering consecutive blocks
parts:
I think Dave's solution is great — rle() is a nice function. It's worth mentioning Bioconductor actually has an Rle class in S4Vectors (created the same way with the Rle() function) that not only calculates runs, but compresses the vector this way (since runs are common in large genomic datasets). If your data are large, I might recommend this.

Also — point of discussion — +1 if dplyr? In my book that's a -0.5! There's something to be said about using base functions when they're there and lead to solutions as readable as dplyr solutions. Dplyr just creates another library dependency and can lead to some horribly obfuscated code in some cases. Its use of special evaluation also creates really nasty complications if you need to do something programmatically. This isn't to say I don't love dplyr — I really do. But base functions have their place. But in my book readability and simplicity are paramount, and for many tasks base R functions fill this role. </rant> :-)

Vince

messages.subject: Re: [D-RUG]: Numbering consecutive blocks
parts:
Vince, 

I agree. It's a useful tool, but I'm starting to run into occasions where the non-standard evaluation is biting me in the butt. Just like here: https://groups.google.com/d/topic/manipulatr/LtSDRL4aOQQ/discussion

Ista points out that the standard evaluation versions of the functions are more universal and programmatic in many cases and it's better to learn those from the start. A bit like learning qplot() only to have to unlearn everything for ggplot(). Base functions are generally less user friendly and the Hadleyverse is generally more so. 

Everything looks like a nail depending on which hammer you're using. 

Brandon
